title: Africa and the text
note: Where the African world meets the biblical record, place by place. Each entry is a set of claims anchored to a site, and every claim names the kind of evidence behind it — an inscription that survives, a text that reports, or a tradition that remembers — and the edition it can be read in. Nothing here is a route, a border or a lineage; what the evidence does not show is said as plainly as what it does.

evidence.inscription: A monument or document from the period, read in a published edition.
evidence.textual: A later written account — a historian, a church writer, a papyrus archive.
evidence.tradition: A memory carried by a community or a text without contemporary confirmation.

claims.text: The Bubastite Portal at Karnak lists about 156 place-names taken by Shoshenq I in a campaign into Canaan, c. 925 BC — the campaign Scripture records under the name Shishak.
claims.source: Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt IV (1906), public domain; plates in Oriental Institute Publications 74 (1954).
claims.limit: Jerusalem is not among the surviving names. The list shows the campaign’s reach, not a march on the city the text describes.

claims.text: The Victory Stela of Piye, set up at Jebel Barkal, records the Kushite conquest of Egypt c. 725 BC — the beginning of the 25th Dynasty, the kings the prophets call Ethiopia.
claims.source: Cairo JE 48862; Breasted, Ancient Records of Egypt IV (1906), public domain.
claims.limit: The stela names Egyptian towns and rulers; it says nothing of Judah.

claims.text: Taharqa — Tirhakah in Kings and Isaiah — built the temple at Kawa; Assyrian records of Esarhaddon and Ashurbanipal name him as their opponent in Egypt.
claims.source: Luckenbill, Ancient Records of Assyria and Babylonia II (1927), public domain in the United States since 2023. The Kawa stelae edition (Macadam, 1949) is in copyright and is cited, not reproduced.
claims.limit: No surviving text places Taharqa at Jerusalem; Kings says only that Sennacherib heard he had come out.

claims.text: Aramaic papyri from the fifth century BC record a Jewish garrison at Yeb with its own temple to YHW, its marriages, contracts and a letter about Passover — a community in Egypt beside the prophets’ Pathros and Syene.
claims.source: Sayce and Cowley, Aramaic Papyri Discovered at Assuan (1906); Cowley, Aramaic Papyri of the Fifth Century B.C. (1923) — both public domain.
claims.limit: The papyri describe this community’s own practice; they do not say when or why it came.

claims.text: Jeremiah addresses Judeans settled at Migdol, Tahpanhes, Noph and in Pathros after the fall of Jerusalem; the prophet himself was taken to Egypt.
claims.limit: The size and fate of these communities are not recorded; the Elephantine archive is the only one that speaks for itself.

claims.text: Apollos, “born at Alexandria, an eloquent man, and mighty in the scriptures,” taught at Ephesus and Corinth; Alexandrian ships carried Paul toward Rome.
Eusebius reports that Mark was the first to be sent to Egypt and founded churches at Alexandria; the Coptic church counts its patriarchs from him.
claims.source: Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 2.16 (NPNF2-01, held); Evetts, History of the Patriarchs of the Coptic Church (1904–15), public domain.
claims.limit: Eusebius writes two and a half centuries later and gives no source; the succession list is the church’s own record of itself.

claims.text: Clement and Origen taught at Alexandria in the late second and third centuries; Athanasius was its bishop. Their works are in the library.
claims.source: Ante-Nicene Fathers 2 and 4; Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers II.4 (held).

claims.text: Simon of Cyrene carried the cross; Cyrenians were at Pentecost, in the synagogue that disputed with Stephen, among the first to preach to Greeks at Antioch; Lucius of Cyrene was a prophet and teacher there.
claims.source: The texts of Mark and Acts.
claims.limit: Whether Rufus and Alexander (Mark 15:21) are the Rufus of Romans 16:13 is not stated by either text.

claims.text: Tertullian wrote at Carthage around 200; Cyprian was its bishop and martyr in 258. Their works, and the account of the martyrs of Scilli and of Perpetua and Felicity, are in the library.
Augustine was bishop of Hippo from 395 to 430; the Confessions and the City of God were written here.
The inscriptions of Ezana, king of Aksum in the fourth century, move from invoking Mahrem and the gods to the formula of the Christian faith — the kingdom’s conversion recorded in its own stone.
claims.source: Littmann, Deutsche Aksum-Expedition IV (1913); English in Budge, A History of Ethiopia (1928) — public domain.
claims.limit: The inscriptions date the conversion of the court; they do not describe how the faith reached it. Rufinus’s story of Frumentius is a later textual account.

claims.text: The Kebra Nagast tells of the Queen of Sheba’s visit to Solomon and of their son Menelik bringing the Ark to Aksum — the founding story of the Ethiopian monarchy.
claims.source: Kebra Nagast, tr. Budge (1922), held in the library.
claims.limit: Tradition. The text of Kings places Sheba’s queen and her gifts; it does not name her country, and the Ark’s later history is not recorded in Scripture.

claims.text: Cosmas, a merchant who sailed to Adulis in the sixth century, copied the inscriptions he found there — the Monumentum Adulitanum — recording Aksumite campaigns in the third century.
claims.source: McCrindle, The Christian Topography of Cosmas (1897), public domain.
claims.limit: The stone itself is lost; the text survives only in Cosmas’s copy.

claims.text: John of Ephesus records the missions of Julian (543) and Longinus (569–575) to Nobatia and the Nubian rulers’ replies; the cathedral of Faras, painted over centuries, was recovered before the lake rose.
claims.source: John of Ephesus, Ecclesiastical History III, tr. Payne Smith (1860); Abu Salih, Churches and Monasteries of Egypt, tr. Evetts (1895) — public domain.
claims.limit: The Ethiopian eunuch of Acts 8 served the Kandake of Meroë, two centuries and more before these missions; the text does not say what became of him.

claims.text: “Candace queen of the Ethiopians” in Acts is a title, Kandake, borne by the ruling queens of Meroë; her treasurer was reading Isaiah on the road from Jerusalem when Philip met him.
claims.source: The text of Acts; the title is attested in Meroitic and classical sources (Pliny, Natural History 6.35).
claims.limit: The eunuch is not named, and no source records his return or a church he founded.

claims.text: Jeremiah was brought here by the remnant of Judah after Gedaliah’s murder, and here he buried stones in the pavement at Pharaoh’s house as a sign of Nebuchadnezzar’s coming.
claims.limit: Petrie’s excavation (1886) identified a fortress platform; whether it is the pavement of the sign is not settled.
